PROCESS

How I work

I find out who we're designing for and what actually stands in their way.

I choose methods based on what the team needs to learn, combine what people say with what they do, and involve users early so decisions rest on evidence and not assumptions.

  • User interviews
  • Expert interviews
  • Contextual inquiry
  • Participant observation
  • Surveys
  • Co-design workshops
  • Design games
  • Heuristic evaluation
  • Competitor analysis

I turn findings into a clear problem, a direction and a way to measure success.

Before any screens are designed, I align product, engineering and stakeholders on who we're solving for, what matters most and what success looks like, so later decisions can be measured against it.

  • Affinity mapping
  • Stakeholder analysis
  • Personas
  • User journey mapping
  • Value Proposition Canvas
  • Problem statements
  • How Might We
  • Prioritisation (MoSCoW)
  • Success criteria & KPIs

I explore broadly, then build the strongest idea into something testable.

I bring the team into ideation so ideas come from more than one discipline, and prototype at the fidelity the question needs, from paper sketches to interactive flows built on reusable components.

  • Crazy 8s
  • Brainwriting
  • Sketching
  • Information architecture
  • User flows
  • Wireframing
  • Interactive prototyping
  • Visual UI design
  • Component libraries

I test while the results can still change the design.

Each round feeds the next iteration. I combine observed behaviour with measured scores, and share findings in a way that leads to decisions.

  • Think-aloud testing
  • Moderated testing
  • Unmoderated remote testing
  • Task success & time on task
  • System Usability Scale (SUS)
  • First-click testing
  • A/B testing
  • Iterative testing

Three years in QA means I design for the details that break in production.

I think about edge cases, error states, devices and accessibility from the first sketch, write designs that can be tested, and check what's built against the design and acceptance criteria before release.

  • Acceptance criteria
  • Test case design
  • Exploratory testing
  • Regression testing
  • Cross-browser & device testing
  • API testing
  • Accessibility testing (WCAG)
  • Bug reporting & triage
  • Design QA & handoff

PROJECT 01
PROJECT 01
UX DESIGN / UI DESIGN / PRODUCT DESIGN - PROJECT 01

DiBU 2.0 - Personalisation as a path to relevance

DiBU 2.0 is a concept for Ældre Sagen's digital user universe, a personalised platform for a Danish membership organisation with over a million members. It's designed for a specific, hard-to-reach group: people in their late fifties and early sixties who are digitally capable but don't yet see themselves in what the organisation offers, because it reads as something for "older people." DiBU 2.0 uses a hybrid personalisation model, part member-controlled and part system-driven, to make the platform feel like it grows with the person as they move from working life into retirement. The result is a platform that meets each member where they are in that transition, turning an organisation they saw as meant for someone older into one that speaks directly to their own life stage.

ROLE
Product Designer (Master's thesis, 3-person team)
MY CONTRIBUTION
Planned and facilitated co-design workshops and interviews, led  and designed the Prototype and the component library
YEAR
2026
INDUSTRY
Nonprofit / Membership & Digital Services
METHODS
Qualitative interviews, participant observation, co-design workshops, iterative prototyping, think-aloud usability testing
UX Design
UI Design
Product Design
Web
View Figma prototype
01 · THE PROBLEM

The members had the skills. They just didn't feel it was for them.

1M+
members in Ældre Sagen
~30%
of members have the digital skills to move online
Jan 2026
physical mail ends in Denmark, and with it the printed magazine

People approaching retirement resist the “pensioner” identity, so Ældre Sagen felt aimed at someone older. Better navigation wouldn't fix that. The problem was perceived relevance, not usability.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

How can personalisation in Ældre Sagen's digital user universe support motivation and perceived relevance among members in the transition from working life to retirement?

02 · THE PROCESS

Co-design with the same members from start to finish

We were a three-person team, and the same informants followed the whole process, from the first interviews to the final tests.

  1. PHASE 1 · DISCOVER
    Understanding the group
    Initial interviews, participant observation at a local branch and a first co-design workshop. This is where the retirement transition surfaced as the design space.
  2. PHASE 2 · DEFINE
    Narrowing the scope
    In-depth interviews to define the target group and scope precisely.
  3. PHASE 3 · DEVELOP
    Three prototype iterations
    System-driven, then user-driven, then hybrid. A second workshop let members prioritise the content for the final version.
  4. PHASE 4 · TEST
    Think-aloud tests
    Six participants, all from earlier in the process, judged whether the concept met the needs they helped identify.
03 · THE INSIGHT

Only a hybrid approach supports all three needs

We mapped each personalisation strategy against the three psychological needs in Self-Determination Theory. User control gives autonomy but risks a filter bubble. System control builds connection but takes away control. A hybrid lets members steer while the system keeps surprising them.

Design choices that support each need

Following the METUX model, each need was translated into concrete choices in the interface and the tasks.

Autonomy
Members feel in control of their own experience.
The way into the personalisation flow is visible, but never required
Members actively choose and deselect their own interests
Personalisation comes from their own choices, not hidden behaviour data
Everything can be adjusted later in Min profil
Competence
Members feel able to navigate and master the platform.
Progressive disclosure introduces complexity gradually
A progress bar gives feedback and prevents overload
Content is pre-sorted by life situation
Min side recalibrates visibly after each input
Relatedness
Members feel connected to others and to a community.
System suggestions sit next to chosen content, to avoid filter bubbles
An interactive map of local activities, placed centrally
Sign-up count and average age shown, so joining alone feels easier
Political polls and applying as volunteer or mentor
04 · THE SOLUTION

Five connected areas, with the member in charge

01Min side

The member's personal front page, which develops with them. On the first visit it shows system-driven recommendations based on age, location and membership data.

A progress indicator invites the member into the personalisation flow without requiring it. After the flow, the page recalibrates so most content follows the member's own choices, while popular items close to their interests keep the selection open. Each recommendation carries a short note on why it's shown.

02Personalisation flow

The bridge between the system-driven and the user-driven parts of the platform. It opens as an overlay from the progress indicator on Min side.

Short steps ask about interests, life situation, advice needs and preferred activities. Every step can be closed without consequences, and the answers update the recommendations right away, so the member sees the effect of their choices.

03Min profil

Direct access to the data and preferences behind the personalisation: chosen interests, signed-up activities and contact details, all editable in one click.

The page also explains what data Ældre Sagen uses and how interests turn into recommendations. Members were willing to share data as long as the purpose was clear.

04Tilbud og aktiviteter

The area for offers and activities, which the research showed was the strongest pull for this group. Activities can be browsed as a list or on an interactive map of the local area.

Labels show whether a suggestion comes from the member's interests or from local popularity. The number signed up and their average age are shown to make it easier to join alone, and members can apply to become a volunteer or mentor.

05Viden og rådgivning

Knowledge and advice for the practical side of the transition: pension, finances, health, legal matters and everyday life.

Content is curated by life situation, so someone five years from retirement sees different guides than someone who has just left work. Search, a life-situation filter and shortcut buttons help members who don't know exactly what to ask.

05 · THE OUTCOME

Six think-aloud tests with participants from the co-design process

WHAT WORKED
  • Participants connected the platform to their own futures.
  • One called the concept younger, with “more substance”. The flow felt like “a help to me”.
  • The activity map and political poll drew the strongest reactions.
WHAT DIDN'T
  • Personalised content wasn't visually distinct, so participants couldn't tell what was tailored to them.
  • Ongoing adjustment was easy to forget.

The tests point to a shift from external motivation, like discounts, toward members linking the platform to their own goals. This shows the design's potential. Whether it lasts would need longitudinal testing.

BEFORE — PLACEMENT BEFORE DIBU 2.0
AFTER — PLACEMENT AFTER DIBU 2.0
06 · REFLECTION

Relevance can't be manufactured with generic content. Give people total control and they shrink their own world, give them none and they resent it. Designing the middle is where the real work was.

Using the same informants throughout gave depth, but they may also have been positive from the start. Next, I'd make personalisation visibly tied to the member's own choices, and test whether the effect holds over time.

END OF CASE 01

PROJECT 02
UX DESIGN / UI DESIGN - PROJECT 02

LMS365 - A skills dashboard that shows learners why a course matters

LMS365 is a learning-management platform built into Microsoft 365, used by large enterprises to train employees. Their skills-management feature was reaching fewer than 10% of eligible customers, so they prepared a case to rethink their methods. Through surveys, expert interviews, and a Value Proposition Canvas, we found that learners stay engaged when they can see why a course matters to their own career. We redesigned the learner dashboard around that idea, resulting in a single screen that shows the gap between your current skills and the ones your job requires, links each gap straight to a relevant course, and lets you push completed skills to your LinkedIn profile. Tested in Maze across two iterations, the final concept scored 81/100 on usability, beating our target of 68, and we backed it with a costed implementation plan and a projected customer-lifetime-value increase of roughly 17%.

ROLE
UX/UI Designer (Group project)
MY CONTRIBUTION
Carried out the survey and expert interviews, co-developed the dashboard concept from the Value Proposition Canvas, prepared the Maze tests and analysed the results.
YEAR
2023
INDUSTRY
B2B SaaS / EdTech / Skills Tech
METHODS
User Research, Personas, Prototyping, Usability Testing
UX Design
UI Design
Product Design
View Figma prototype
01 · THE PROBLEM

A skills tool that fewer than 1 in 10 eligible customers used

<10%
of Professional Plan customers used the skills-management feature
~50%
of LMS365's customers are on the Professional Plan
500+
employees at a typical LMS365 customer

Skills management is becoming a standard requirement for learning platforms, and competitors like MuchSkills and Bridge already offered strong visual tools for learners. We focused on the learners rather than the companies buying the platform, because their engagement decides whether the feature gets used.

PROBLEM STATEMENT

How can we increase LMS365's customers' engagement through a redesign of the skills management function?

02 · THE PROCESS

From a broad brief to a tested concept in four phases

We were a five-person team at ITU with LMS365 as case partner, working under an NDA.

  1. PHASE 1 · DISCOVER
    Framing the problem
    Stakeholder analysis, competitor research, LMS365's internal documents, a survey and two expert interviews with HR and e-learning professionals.
  2. PHASE 2 · DEFINE
    Two learner profiles
    A Value Proposition Canvas turned the findings into two personas, Dwight and Jim, and three design criteria with measurable success targets.
  3. PHASE 3 · DEVELOP
    Sketching and prototyping
    Brainwriting 6-3-5 to generate ideas, then an interactive Figma prototype built into LMS365's existing platform.
  4. PHASE 4 · TEST
    Two iterations in Maze
    Remote usability tests with tasks, SUS, Likert scales and free-text questions. Iteration 1 felt cluttered and hid the LinkedIn feature, so iteration 2 moved it into the skills matrix and grouped content into clear boxes.
03 · THE INSIGHT

Both personas needed to see why a course matters

Our two personas wanted very different things from the platform, but both stay engaged when it shows how a course connects to their own job.

PERSONA · DWIGHT
Ambitious and career-driven
Wants recognition, certificates and a concrete path forward, and wants to follow his own development.
PERSONA · JIM
Does what's required
Has no interest in career development. Wants to finish the mandatory courses with as little effort as possible.
USER FLOW: FROM REQUIRED SKILL TO COURSE TO MANAGER MEETING
04 · THE SOLUTION

A dashboard that links every skills gap to a course

01Dashboard

The first screen after login, replacing LMS365's “My Training Dashboard”. It shows the learner's work title, a progress indicator and the required skills they haven't completed yet.

Each required skill is clickable and leads to courses that close the gap. Below, a skills matrix compares the current and required level for each skill, so the learner sees their personal skills gap at a glance.

02Course overlay and skills tags

Clicking a required skill opens an overlay with matching courses.

Every course carries skills tags showing which skills it teaches and at what level. The tags also drive the course recommendations, which answered a wish from the survey for easier ways to find the right course.

03Course catalog

All courses in one place: enrolled, saved and completed.

Filters on the left include skills, so learners can browse by the skill they want to build instead of by course name.

04LinkedIn and Teams

Learners can add a skill to their LinkedIn profile in one click, but only once they've reached the required level, so the skill reflects real learning.

When all required skills for a work title are met, a button opens Microsoft Teams to book a review with their manager, turning completed learning into a conversation about the next step.

05 · THE OUTCOME

Two of four targets met, and the other two were close

We tested the second iteration in Maze against the design criteria from the Value Proposition Canvas.

CRITERION 1 · OVERVIEW
SUS score for finding a course through required skills
TARGET
68 / 100
RESULT
81 / 100
Met
CRITERION 2 · ENGAGEMENT
Participants who saw that more than four skills were required
TARGET
75%
RESULT
82%
Met
CRITERION 2 · ENGAGEMENT
Ease of adding a skill to LinkedIn, on a 1–7 scale
TARGET
4.7
RESULT
4.6
Just below. Quick to do, but hard to find at first
CRITERION 3 · CONNECTION
Sentiment of feedback on how work title and required skills connect
TARGET
0.60
RESULT
0.52
Just below. The tool rated phrases like “makes sense” as neutral

The business case

We estimated the cost from LMS365's agile setup, 298 story points across 15 sprints with three developers, and calculated the effect on customer lifetime value.

3.1M DKK
estimated implementation cost
~3.2%
of LMS365's ARR growth target for 2024–25
+16.6%
projected customer lifetime value per Professional Plan customer by 2026
WHAT WORKED
  • Participants found that the link between work title and required skills made sense.
  • Adding a skill to LinkedIn was fast once participants found the feature.
  • LMS365's feedback was mostly positive, and they were satisfied with the rationale behind the concept.
WHAT LMS365 QUESTIONED
  • Whether the solution is realistic, given how central Microsoft 365 is to their platform.
  • How skills would be verified, and the data structures needed behind them.
06 · REFLECTION

The first iteration failed in a useful way. Testers couldn't find the LinkedIn feature and the screen felt cluttered. Grouping the content into a clear hierarchy and moving LinkedIn into the skills matrix is what lifted the second iteration. An engagement problem is often a clarity problem.

Our research was thin on learners. We ran only two interviews, both with people in creator roles, and testing started late. Next time I'd involve learners directly and test earlier. We also underestimated how much LMS365 depends on Microsoft 365, which is exactly what they questioned in their feedback.

END OF CASE 02

UX DESIGN / UI DESIGN / HAI - PROJECT 03

VESA - A verified source assistant to minimise the spread of misinformation

VESA is a concept tool that lives inside a Facebook group for alternative medicine and helps members back up their claims with credible sources. It suggests verified articles as people write, lets them earn a trust badge by passing a short comprehension check, and never forces anyone to add a source. The goal is to raise the quality of information without turning a warm, experience-driven community into a policed one.

ROLE
UX/UI Designer (Group project)
MY CONTRIBUTION
Conducted the semi-structured interviews with community members, took part in both rounds of Crazy 8 ideation, and designed the visual UI of the prototype, including the source suggestion and verification flows.
YEAR
2025
INDUSTRY
Health & Wellness, Social Platforms, Information tech
METHODS
Heuristic evaluation, interviews, data-driven personas, wireframing, usability testing
UX Design
UI Design
Product Design
01 · THE PROBLEM

Welcoming communities, but fertile ground for misinformation

Facebook groups for alternative medicine run on personal experience and peer recommendations. Members can post claims without any evidence, and many already feel overlooked by conventional healthcare. The brief was to design an LLM-based solution that reduces misinformation without breaking the community's dynamics.

DESIGN CHALLENGE 1
Don't kill the community
Avoid choices that discourage members from taking part.
DESIGN CHALLENGE 2
Don't make the AI an authority
Guide and improve information quality without acting as a censor.
DESIGN CHALLENGE 3
Balance community and quality
Support credible sharing while keeping questions and experiences open.
HOW MIGHT WE

How might we encourage users in the online community for alternative medicine to share trustworthy knowledge, so Annie feels content and reassured?

02 · THE PROCESS

Three phases, from evaluating an existing AI to testing our own

We were a five-person team, and everyone contributed equally across all three phases.

  1. PHASE 1 · EVALUATE
    Heuristic evaluation of Doctor AI
    Three tasks in ChatGPT's Doctor AI, evaluated with Nielsen's heuristics and Amershi et al.'s human-AI guidelines. It revealed missing sources, hidden system limits, an inconsistent tone and a biased default voice.
  2. PHASE 2 · RESEARCH
    Interviews and personas
    Six semi-structured interviews with community members, analysed with Cooper's 7-step method into two personas and a How Might We question.
  3. PHASE 3 · IDEATE
    Crazy 8s and a journey map
    Two rounds of Crazy 8s, the second one sketched instead of written, followed by wireframes and a user journey map for our primary persona.
  4. PHASE 4 · TEST
    Two rounds of think-aloud tests
    A mid-fidelity Figma prototype, tested first to find usability issues and then to validate the revised design. We also tested the AI's prompt logic for failure cases.
03 · THE INSIGHT

Members wanted credibility, but on their own terms

The interviews gave us two personas with opposite needs. Designing for Lea would have meant strong AI authority and moderation, which would harm the experience-sharing that Annie and the community rely on. We chose Annie.

PRIMARY PERSONA · ANNIE
Believes in it, and wants evidence
A 60-year-old holistic nutritionist who values other members' experiences but also wants evidence-based knowledge.
PERSONA · LEA
Sceptical, but curious
A 40-year-old professor who follows the group passively and is frustrated by misinformation and easily searchable questions.

From challenges to design responses

Each design response in VESA comes from a problem we found in Doctor AI and a need we found in the interviews.

PHASE 1 · AI CHALLENGE
What we found in Doctor AI
Lack of transparency: no sources or explanations provided
Poor communication: the system overpromised its capabilities
Inconsistent tone: a casual tone reduced medical credibility
Risk of overreliance: uncertain outputs shown with high confidence
PHASE 2 · USER NEED
What Annie needs
Evidence-based knowledge without losing the community's supportive tone
Clarity and reassurance, to avoid misinformation
A warm community, and no overly authoritative systems
A way to tell personal experience from credible knowledge
PHASE 3 · DESIGN RESPONSE
What VESA does
Transparent source suggestions with clear links to the original sources
Clear communication when no valid sources are available
A supportive, non-authoritative tone with optional interaction
User-driven verification through a short review step that earns a badge
04 · THE SOLUTION

A verified source assistant inside the post and comment flow

01Source suggestions as you write

After a member writes a post or comment, VESA highlights key words in purple and opens a pop-up with article cards from verified sources.

Each card shows a title, a short description and an image, so the member can judge relevance at a glance. More than three articles appear in a carousel, keeping the overview clear without breaking the writing flow.

02Verify and earn a badge

After choosing an article, the member reads it and answers a short test. Three correct answers verify the source and add a badge to the article card.

The friction is intentional. It asks members to evaluate the AI's suggestion instead of accepting it blindly, and signals credibility to others in the group.

03Add your own source

Members who already trust a source can paste the link themselves.

The post is published with a verified source label and a badge, without the test, on the assumption that the member already knows the content.

04When no valid source exists

VESA only suggests sources from approved, credible publications. When it can't find one, a dropdown explains why.

The member can still publish. Showing the limitation keeps expectations realistic instead of letting the AI overpromise.

05Posting without a source

VESA never requires a source. Questions, experiences and discussions can be posted freely, and question posts are left untouched.

Before posting without a source, a subtle reminder appears. Every pop-up can be closed, so the member stays in control.

05 · THE OUTCOME

Testers valued the friction, but warned it could cost participation

Before user testing, we tested the prompt logic in Gemini, Doctor AI and ChatGPT to see how the AI would fail.

9 in 10
AI source suggestions were useful and correct
1 in 10
were off-topic or had fabricated titles, so the concept had to handle that failure
WHAT WORKED
  • Testers saw the verification step as valuable, because it made them reflect before sharing.
  • Participants responded positively when VESA admitted it couldn't find a valid source.
  • Letting members verify sources turned the AI's failure rate into a reason to engage with the sources.
WHAT TO IMPROVE
  • The friction might discourage some members from posting.
  • Failure and edge cases needed clearer system behaviour and visual hierarchy.
  • Scientific articles can be too complex for everyday community use.
06 · REFLECTION

Friction isn't automatically bad. A short verification step made members reflect before sharing, without making them feel controlled. The hard part is the balance: if validation becomes too demanding, people stop contributing, and the community loses the knowledge sharing we wanted to support.

Transparency cuts both ways. A label like “unverified post” builds trust in information, but can also stigmatise the poster and clash with the community's norms. Next, I'd test softer ways to communicate uncertainty, and look for sources that are both credible and easy to read.

END OF CASE 03

UX DESIGN / UI DESIGN - PROJECT 04

Surround Festival - One platform for visitors, musicians and volunteers

Surround is a free, nonprofit, fully volunteer-run music festival in Roskilde, Denmark. Recruiting and keeping volunteers was hard, and communication scattered across Messenger, Facebook and email meant tasks slipped through the cracks. Working with the all-year volunteers as design partners, we redesigned the festival's single-page site into a six-page platform that gives volunteers one hub for their work, and makes volunteering more appealing through titled, CV-worthy positions.

ROLE
UX/UI Designer (Group project)
MY CONTRIBUTION
Observed the volunteers' internal meeting and interviewed a co-leader, took part in the design games and ideation, and designed the visual UI of the six-page prototype.
YEAR
2023
INDUSTRY
Nonprofit / Events / Music festival
METHODS
Co-design, Research, Personas, Prototyping, Usability Testing
UX Design
UI Design
Web
View Figma prototype
01 · THE PROBLEM

A volunteer-run festival that struggled to recruit and coordinate

100%
volunteer-run, free and nonprofit
~15
all-year volunteers planning the festival
3
platforms for internal planning: Messenger, Facebook and email

Surround is a free, volunteer-run festival in Roskilde that presents upcoming artists, with a focus on diversity. A core team always showed up while other volunteers came and went, and with planning spread across several platforms, tasks were left unfinished close to the festival.

DESIGN OPENING

A redesign of Surround's website that makes volunteering more appealing to new members and gives the current volunteers one place to plan.

02 · THE PROCESS

Co-designed with the volunteers in three steps

I worked in a team of six, with Surround's all-year volunteers as design partners from the first observation to the final test.

  1. PHASE 1 · RESEARCH
    Observing how the festival is planned
    We joined an internal planning meeting, documented it on video and interviewed co-leader Caroline about the festival and its volunteers.
  2. PHASE 2 · WORKSHOP
    Design games on motivation
    A persona game and a stakeholder mapping game on motivation, responsibility, time and social atmosphere, followed by interviews with co-leader Astrid and a new volunteer.
  3. PHASE 3 · CO-DESIGN AND TEST
    Building the website together
    The volunteers assembled a website from cut-out pieces of our redesign. Then Caroline tested the Figma prototype while thinking aloud.
03 · THE INSIGHT

Not every volunteer is there for the same reason

In the persona game, each volunteer built their own volunteer persona from icons like community, music, career and networking, and rated how much each mattered. Their motives were very different, and several were career-driven. That changed how we saw recruitment.

From findings to design responses

Each part of the redesign comes from something the volunteers told us or showed us.

WHAT WE FOUND
The problem
Recruiting new volunteers, and keeping them for a whole year, is a constant struggle
Young volunteers increasingly look for skills and titles they can use
Planning is spread across Messenger, Facebook and email, and tasks go unfinished
The volunteers want the festival's story and people to be visible
WHERE IT CAME FROM
The source
Interviews with Caroline and Astrid
The persona game, and Emilie in workshop 2
The interview with Astrid
The interview with Caroline and the website-building activity
DESIGN RESPONSE
What the website does
A volunteer page that presents open roles as positions to apply for
Named positions that can go on a CV, LinkedIn or a grant application
A log-in hub with a shared task board and calendar
Volunteer portraits and stories, a values section and artist teasers
04 · THE SOLUTION

A six-page website for visitors, volunteers and musicians

01Landing page

The old site was one long page. The new landing page keeps only what the volunteers said mattered most.

A banner with the logo, the dates and a link to the map, followed by a teaser of this year's artists, information about the festival, mood pictures and behind-the-scenes videos.

02Volunteer page

A page dedicated to volunteering that opens with the current volunteers: who they are and what they do.

Below, “Become a volunteer” describes what it means to volunteer at Surround, followed by “Positions available”. A title for each role makes volunteering easier to understand and something you can put on LinkedIn. The volunteers debated whether “position” was the right word, since it didn't quite match how they see their work.

03Log-in hub

A personal landing page for volunteers, with their tasks sorted into To do, In progress and Done, and a calendar of internal meetings and events.

Volunteers can assign and unassign tasks, so everyone can see who is responsible and how far a task has come. If someone gets busy, another volunteer can take over, so no one is irreplaceable.

04Music program

A special request from the volunteers, made for both visitors and musicians.

This year's artists with music teasers and social links, the program from previous years, and a section where musicians can send in their music. In workshop 2, the volunteers asked for song snippets right on the site.

05Map

Practical information for visitors: a map of the festival area in Roskilde with toilets, food and transport.

Below are the three stages, Roskilde Domkirke, Havescenen and Byscenen. Each one opens a description and the artists playing there.

06FAQ and values

The existing FAQ content in a clearer design.

We added a values section, because the volunteers wanted visitors to see what Surround stands for.

05 · THE OUTCOME

The volunteers started planning to use the redesign

At the end of the final session, the volunteers started discussing how to bring elements of the redesign into their existing website. They had wanted to change it for a long time but didn't know how.

CAROLINE TESTING THE FIGMA PROTOTYPE
WHAT WORKED
  • The persona game made the leaders aware that volunteers have different motives, a conversation they said they needed.
  • Building the website from paper pieces let the volunteers shape the design directly.
  • The activity surfaced concrete requests, like song snippets on the artist pages and more personal volunteer profiles.
06 · REFLECTION

Working with volunteers means designing for people who aren't obliged to show up. That applied to our process as much as to the product, and it's why the redesign focuses on making commitment visible and work easy to hand over.

With a client like this, I'd agree on time and participation from the start, and time-box each workshop activity so the most valuable part, making things together, gets the most time.

END OF CASE 04

BRANDING / GRAPHIC DESIGN - PROJECT 05

EM Nordic - Brand and campaign design for a music retailer

EM Nordic is a Danish music-instrument supplier selling gear across the full spectrum of music and production, from guitars and microphones to audio interfaces, effects pedals, and studio equipment. As a graphic and UX student worker, I built brand and campaign material that made a broad, technical catalogue feel cohesive and desirable. That work spanned two connected pieces, a themed sublogo system representing each product category, and a library of product-showcase visuals designed to sell those products across Instagram and Facebook.

ROLE

01 · SUBLOGO SYSTEM

One logo, a variant for every product category

As a part-time graphic and UX student worker, I produced brand assets, campaign material and social media content for EM Nordic. For the sublogo system, I turned the "em nordic" logo into a flexible set of themed variants, each weaving an instrument motif into the letterforms, from a guitar and a mixing console to drumsticks, keys, marimba bars and a DJ setup. Each variant maps to a product category, so content signals what it's about before a word is read, while staying clearly the same brand.

02 · EMINENTE ARTISTER

From a sticker-like badge to a mark that sits on a photo

The Eminente Artister redesign started from EM Nordic's previous sponsored-artist mark, a round badge that read as a sticker on top of artist photos. I opened it into a freer composition, keeping the red and black, the script lettering and the red sweep, but letting the sweep wrap around the wordmark so it sits on a photo without boxing it in.

BEFORE — PREVIOUS EMINENTE ARTISTER LOGO
AFTER — REDESIGNED EMINENTE ARTISTER LOGO
03 · CAMPAIGN POSTS

The system applied across product campaigns

For the campaign visuals, I applied the system across product campaigns, composing each product into a branded scene with the matching sublogo, and producing every post in both Facebook and Instagram formats.

ABOUT

Michelle Birkkjær Nielsen

I'm a digital product designer working where user experience, engineering and business meet. Alongside my studies at ITU, I've worked in QA at IMPACT Commerce for three years, testing real client platforms for functionality, compatibility and accessibility. That work shapes how I design. I think about edge cases, handoff and technical feasibility from the first sketch, not as an afterthought. I specialise in human-AI interaction and personalisation, and I do my best work when I can own a solution from research to finished concept, close to the team building it.
